Sources indicate that hi, I’m Papa George! In my 69 years I’ve done a lot of cool things – I’ve crossed the Atlantic in a 40-foot sailboat, bushwacked 100 miles across the north slope of the Alaska Range, hiked for 26 days in Western Nepal crossing five passes over 5,000 meters, and climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years. I have been active in retirement, and I hiked the Wonderland Trail in 2024 and the Long Trail in 2025. This year I'm trying... the John Muir Trail!

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

According to recent reports, the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

Industry observers note that “He was really lucky,” noted Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

It has been revealed that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#125167. Completing The Collection

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1024 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Completing The Collection

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that completing my double hike of the AT isn’t the only commitment I am devoted to keeping.
  • In a recent development, around midnight it hit me.
  • In a recent development, I remainder tucked under my quilt, even going so far as to eat my breakfast inside its cozy confines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that completing my double hike of the AT isn’t the only commitment I am devoted to keeping. I check the box on another one despite a chilly morning.

In a recent development, around midnight it hit me. I was camping practically at the northbound 1,200 mile marker. I hadn’t seen a marker yesterday, so it fell to me to whip one up on my way out of camp so I could my collection. This wasn’t ideal, it was barely above freezing. Every part of me wanted to stay in my tent as long as possible. When it did come time to hit the trail, I would want to get moving and stay moving, preferably all the way back to my van. My silly rituals will probably be my undoing some day.

In a recent development, I remainder tucked under my quilt, even going so far as to eat my breakfast inside its cozy confines. I am continually impressed how well the down insulates and warms me. I feel like I’d be warm in 20 degree weather, maybe even lower. I don’t intend to ever camp in such weather, but to know it’s possible is exactly what I had in mind when I purchased this particular quilt. It kept my warm until 7:45AM when I initiated my pack up procedure, completing the various tasks by 8:00AM, the cold having motivated me to move fast.

According to recent reports, I checked in at the Showers Steps viewpoint since it was just a handful of steps away. It sure looked like I’d made the right choice to prioritize sunset the previous night, there wouldn’t have been much to see at sunrise given the heavy cloud cover to start the day. I located the 1,200 mile point on the trail to the tenth of a mile and quickly pieced together a small marker. It wouldn’t last long, but I just needed a photo for my collection so I can sleep at night. I am planning to post them all in a blog post, along with other notable milestones like state lines after my hike.

My thin gloves were doing little to warm my fingers, but other than that I was comfortable even with the temperature sitting in the mid 30s. South of Showers Steps the trail briefly winds amongst some mountain laurels, which, unlike rocks, are in fact the state flower of Pennsylvania. A few miles later I crossed route 501 and approached the Kimmel Lookout. I spent a moment or two setting up a picture or two before whipping around and continuing down the trail. I didn’t realize it until it came time to put together today’s blog, but one of the pictures turned out kind of epic. The early morning sun radiates through clouds above speckling its light across the rocky ledge and trees. Colorful late fall trees poke up from the ground below the ledge with large meadows and farms visible further in the distance.

Early morning view from the Showers Steps.

The 1,200 mile marker, my collection is complete!

The view from the Kimmel Lookout. I think I’ll hang on to this one.

I followed the same ridge for the next 10 miles to Swatara Gap. Although it was a Saturday, it had been relatively quite on trail. I only passed a trio of hunters on the trail before encountering a lively group of women at a viewpoint along the trail. One of them had just had an interesting experience a short distance down the trail. She had stepped off the trail for a restroom break only to find out after the fact that a hunter had been just overhead on a tree stand the entire time. She didn’t seem nearly as put off by the experience as I would have been. The discussion moved to my double AT attempt. I wish I could have gotten a picture of their reaction upon hearing what I was up to. They were even more impressed that I was essentially in the final week of the task. I forgot to tell them that FarOut commenters frequently mentioned a family of 5 or so copperheads hanging out on the rocks we were all standing on, though I believe they aren’t keen on cold temperatures and were probably in hiding.

Soon I was making my way back down to Swatara Gap and under Interstate 81. I made it the final mile back to my van before 2:00PM. After cleaning up and trimming my increasingly beardy face, I headed to Lebanon, PA to complete yesterday and today’s blog posts as has become my usual routine. There is no Formula One tomorrow so I am not sure what to do with myself, I haven’t have a Sunday morning free from blog writing or sports watching in a while. I am sure I’ll think of something.

A lookout north of Swatara Gap.

A glimpse of I-81 from the trail just north of Swatara Gap.

Passing beneath I-81 on the AT.

Total: 15.8 miles, 32,344 steps.

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • Sources indicate that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

Sources indicate that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Industry observers note that ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed initiative.

Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#125159. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1683 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to initiative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to initiative. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

It has been revealed that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Sources indicate that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

According to recent reports, for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

According to recent reports, by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

According to recent reports, I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

Industry observers note that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

It has been revealed that I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

It has been revealed that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

According to recent reports, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Recent findings suggest that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

In a recent development, the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

Recent findings suggest that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

#125158. Latest Update: A Night with a Camino Ghost

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (924 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Night with a Camino Ghost

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we slept surprisingly well last night, even though our room sat directly above a lively bar.
  • Sources indicate that with the window shutters closed, we blocked out all the street noise.
  • This morning, I walked out to the kitchen and opened the tall doors leading to the courtyard to let the cool air in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we slept surprisingly well last night, even though our room sat directly above a lively bar. People partied and ate dinner late into the night. That is completely normal here, as most businesses close for siesta and do not reopen until after 8:00 PM.

Sources indicate that with the window shutters closed, we blocked out all the street noise. Unfortunately, closing them also trapped the heat inside, making the room quite warm.

This morning, I walked out to the kitchen and opened the tall doors leading to the courtyard to let the cool air in. I made a cup of coffee and ate fresh blueberries with yogurt.

In a recent development, because it was Sunday morning, the street noise was minimal. Listening to the seagulls and mourning doves while sipping coffee was a peaceful way to start the day.

We finally set off at 9:00 AM. Pontevedra is a good-sized city with an intact medieval center, so it took us a little while to walk out of town. Before long, however, we found ourselves back on a quiet country road.

The Camino wound alongside a river before merging onto a paved road. We took the road route, which was poorly marked, but we soon reconnected with the main trail. Along the way, we passed hundreds of pilgrims heading in the opposite direction toward Santiago.

From there, the trail entered the woods and began to climb. It got quite steep for a short stretch before leveling out into a pleasant forest path. We hiked downhill over rocky terrain, passing cool, shaded creeks along the way.

Eventually, we emerged into Pontesampaio, a well-kept medieval village. We wound our way through its narrow alleyways down to a wide river. To cross, we had to wait our turn on a narrow, 300-foot arched stone bridge, letting oncoming cars pass before we walked across.

Once across, we stopped at a local restaurant serving ultra-fresh food. I ordered grilled squid that had just come off the docks that morning, and the restaurant even harvests its own chickens. Best of all, the meal was a fraction of what it would cost back in the States.

After a relaxing siesta lunch, we still had about 7.5 kilometers (4.6 miles) left to hike.

As we walked through several connected medieval neighborhoods, the Camino suddenly split into two routes:.

At first, the split confused me, and seeing the mountain crest ahead was intimidating because we were already hot and tired. Fortunately, we chose the shorter Coastal route, and the trail skirted the side of the mountain rather than going straight over the top.

Industry observers note that however, the descent brought us onto the shoulder of a busy highway. We endured two miserable miles of roaring traffic and exhaust fumes before finally reaching Redondela.

Redondela felt a bit rundown in spots, though it features a charming medieval quarter beneath a massive, 100-foot-tall iron train trestle.

We arrived at our apartment at 4:00 PM, completely exhausted. Our host was wonderful and had prepared a special herbal tea for us to soak our feet. The recipe belonged to his grandmother, who was actually the very first pharmacist in Redondela. (Unlike in the States, pharmacists in Spain can prescribe and dispense many medications without a doctor’s visit.).

It has been revealed that while soaking our feet, we drank some mediocre Spanish wine. Because it was Sunday afternoon, almost everything was closed except for a small mini-market with limited options.

Sources indicate that later, we visited a local bakery our host recommended. Hikers always love talking about food—when you are burning thousands of calories a day, you rapidly get tired of trail snacks and start dreaming about town food. We loaded up on a few local treats:.

After the bakery, we wandered through the narrow alleyways of the old city, admiring the elevated rail bridge towering overhead. By 8:00 PM, the town came alive as bars and restaurants reopened after siesta.

Sources indicate that this time, the waitress brought out two small bowls of white noodles soaked in olive oil with bread on the side. The noodles had dark streaks of squid ink running down them, adding a mild, salty seafood flavor.

It has been revealed that exhausted from the long walk, we headed back to the apartment. Our host had preserved the space just as his grandmother left it—it truly felt like she still lived there. We threw the windows wide open to let the cool night air roll in and fell fast asleep, though it felt like Grandma’s presence lingered in the room all night long.

Industry News: No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (383 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • It has been revealed that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is promptly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

It has been revealed that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

In a recent development, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

Latest Update: Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (341 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

It has been revealed that eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

Industry observers note that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He stated climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

In a recent development, the Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” remarked Kondrashkin.

According to recent reports, the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

In a recent development, on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#125145. Day 38: The Last Full Day Before Santiago

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1087 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Day 38: The Last Full Day Before Santiago

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knowing it was the last big walking day before Santiago, I got up early and started under the stars.
  • The shadow of the trees made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, but I leaned into the challenge.
  • I wove in and out of towns, trying to find a cafe that was open, but every single one I passed was closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowing it was the last big walking day before Santiago, I got up early and started under the stars.

The shadow of the trees made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, but I leaned into the challenge.

My legs had been consistently sore for a week.

And yet, I didn’t want to stop walking.

As the sun came up, though, so did my mood.

I wove in and out of towns, trying to find a cafe that was open, but every single one I passed was closed. Many of the restaurants and albergues were closing for the season. In a way, it felt like we were politely being asked to “wrap it up.”.

Sources indicate that well, a beautiful stone-walled restaurant was my savior. The WiFi network was called “A Cova de Meiga” (a cove of the witch), and it felt like a warm sanctuary.

A fire in the corner, old sewing machines and instruments on the wall, and the restaurant owner’s two young boys brought a childlike joy to my morning.

My Argentinian brother found me there and we shared a tarta de Santiago with our coffees as we warmed up by the fire.

After that cafe, we made it two kilometers before we found our Italian brother at another cafe.

He asked if we wanted anything, and even though we all had just stopped, I suggested we get another coffee and take the day very slowly.

They were more than happy with that idea, and we all sat with another round of café con leche while we shared a tortilla.

When we started walking, silence rapidly became the conversation.

The presence of the moment felt potent as we saw the trail markers giving a countdown.

Each leaf glowing with the wind.

The smell of pine from the needles I crushed in my hand.

The chill of the wind combined with the warmth of the sun.

Every detail felt more vibrant because it was the last full day.

In O Pedrouzo, we decided to stop again for lunch. With a table full of food at the Mexican restaurant, A Catriña, we talked and ate and talked and ate.

There were still 15 out of the 36 kilometers to do, so together we set out into the afternoon sun.

We walked through what felt like a magical forest, with everything around us was alive with the most intense colors of green. Like little kids, we hugged the trees, climbed them, and hung from their bark.

It has been revealed that once we hit the trail marker that read we were under ten kilometers, I saw my Italian brother put a sticker on the column. I stopped next to him and he suggested we walk together till the end. In agreement, I plopped on the road to wait for our third. A few minutes later, our Argentinian brother jumped on us in greeting. We lay there in that spot, soaking up the reality of being so close to Santiago.

Recent findings suggest that together, side-by-side-by-side, we finished the last stretch of the day. Our strides naturally matching, we marched onward, each taking turns singing our country’s national anthems. It felt like our individual patriotism fed the energy of the group. The exact energy boost we needed for the end.

At the municipal albergue in Monte de Gozo, the Pilgrims Hostel was basically a compound. We were in a building labeled 29, and the others were in a terraced line down the descent. They were newly constructed, and there were enough to fit 400 pilgrims. We only ended up with 9 pilgrims on the whole property.

Nearby at the pilgrim monument overlooking Santiago, the three of us caught the sunset at the perfect time as it was about to go over the horizon. I couldn’t believe I was looking at the cathedral that we’d talked about for so long. Leaning against the metal monument, I cried for the end of the journey.

Tomorrow, I’d touch that cathedral.

Industry observers note that sitting on the hill, I realized I felt more present and at peace today than I had for most of my life. Then it hit me….

Those had been my intentions for the year, and tomorrow starts a new cycle of intentions.

Our last full night was spent making a steep descent to the grocery store just to climb back up and eat.

In a recent development, our Italian brother entertained the pilgrims in the kitchen. He ate hot dogs raw while he cooked fish sticks in the microwave, initially thinking they were chicken and didn’t need to be fried. They did need to be fried.

According to recent reports, one of the girls from Germany had been carrying a candle for her whole Camino. She had only used it once, but in celebration of my upcoming birthday, she lit it and set it in front of me to make a pre-birthday wish. How special.

Sources indicate that once everyone was done eating, we played Uno with seven people. The four other people had walked different Caminos (the Primitivo and the Norte) and weren’t as accustomed to the crowds. To us, the numbers in the albergue were few, so getting to hear different stories and perspectives was fascinating.

Sources indicate that I laughed the perfect amount for the last night. It was joyful.

#125143. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (612 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Recent findings suggest that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Recent findings suggest that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My strategy is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he stated.

According to recent reports, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Industry observers note that neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Industry observers note that lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch looks to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line at the moment being attempted by a Russian team.

In a recent development, this is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

In a recent development, kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#125141. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1235 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Industry observers note that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It revealed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Industry observers note that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang mentioned: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

It has been revealed that strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

In a recent development, “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

In a recent development, during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

Industry observers note that “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

In a recent development, “Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

According to recent reports, “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

Industry observers note that “We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

In a recent development, the climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

In a recent development, the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

In a recent development, on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

In a recent development, the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#125138. New Mexico is the reward

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1821 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

New Mexico is the reward

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The library is a bit chaotic, all the books are in the process of being boxed up for a move.
  • I wanted to do some blogging but turns out the library closes for lunch.
  • In true CDT fashion its covered in barbed wire and bones!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The library is a bit chaotic, all the books are in the process of being boxed up for a move. I ask when they are moving and where to. The librarian doesn’t know herself. There are two computers there which Brokeback and i jump on to fill out our NDA permit forms. There isn’t any clear guidance on how to fill them out, so we call Fort Huachua and ask some questions. The person who answers say i need to have an active service member, veteran or DOD contractor as a sponsor. This doesn’t seem to add up to what the CDTC claims about international hikers, we just need to be with a US citizen who also had the permit. So i skip this on the form. We go into a back room with whitish walls to take pictures  for the permit. Mine is pretty bad! I compile all the documents and send everything off to the Fort Huachuca email. Fingers crossed!

I wanted to do some blogging but turns out the library closes for lunch. Brokeback and i walk back into town. Chama is a pretty long town that stretches along the road, so its a while. I drop into the grocery store to get more of my resupply. There i meet Tim & Cassie again. They are staying with JJ and invite me to come over for a dinner they are cooking. I say yes, and after finishing we walk back into town. We spend the afternoon hanging out with the rest of the Oysters outside the Iron Rail Inn. Later we walk over to JJ’s with Tim & Cassie. There we make dinner together and chat for a good while. I also get to peek around the Exoticpax  and Aardwolf production rooms. Its pretty cool getting to see their setups as someone who also makes gear.

In true CDT fashion its covered in barbed wire and bones!

The dusk sky near Lagunitas lake.

Groves of golden Aspen were very common on this part of the trail.

Industry observers note that its pretty cold overnight, and at about 5am I’m awake. There’s frost on the ground and so after heading off to dig my morning cathole, i decide to pack up and start hiking in the dark. I reach the edge of the mesa we are on shortly after dawn and am treated to views of the pine forests below.

Looking down towards Abiquiu in the morning.

Industry observers note that after this the trail descends down towards Ghost Ranch and pretty quickly the landscape changes from pine forest to something more arid. Its when we reach the Arroyo del Yeso that we get our first true sense of being in the desert!

Our first true view of the Upcoming Mexico desert near Ghost Ranch.

Every September Albuquerque hosts the hot air balloon fiesta. Back in Chama we decided to go if we could get tickets. Its a couple of hours drive, through a desert landscape. I look around as we drive and wonder if this is what the rest of Latest Mexico is going to be like.

We get tickets for the morning session, so wake up at about 4am the next day. I feel pretty awful on the short car ride over. By the time we are walking into the Arena i start to feel pretty excited, and after getting coffee i feel pretty good. I imagined we would be in a viewing area away from the balloon. However you get to walk in among them as they set up which was so cool! The first balloons lifted off just before sunrise to the strains of the US National Anthem. After this its was a constant stream of balloons being inflated and lifting off! There must have been around 100 balloons in the air at one point. 2027 SOBO’s, this is one amazing sidequest!

The first balloons lifting off before dawn.

According to recent reports, after leaving the festival we got breakfast and then napped back at the hotel. Did some laundry and just hung out for the rest of the day. Later we drove to an all you can eat sushi restaurant and demolished many rolls!

Sources indicate that while visiting Albuqerque had been fun, it was definitely a little overwhelming to be in such a significant city. So i was glad to be heading back to trail. Tengram dropped us off at Ghost Ranch around midday. He was going to camp with us that evening so we put camping bits in his car and get slacked again.

The crew hiking out towards the Rio Chama.

The route out of Ghost Ranch is pretty nice, and goes on a piece of the land that you usually don’t get to access. Now there were substantial sandstone cliffs in almost all directions and it felt like we were truly in the desert. We crossed the highway and followed the dirt road up alongside the Rio Chama towards where the Ghost Ranch Alt rejoins the redline. Halfway along there is a campsite where Tengram is setup. We gather for dinner and then the projector comes out for the Second Twilight Movie! I enjoy it in a its so bad its good kind of way.

In a recent development, the others in the Oysters were going to do a backyard ultra to Cuba the next day, about 50 miles. I decided that this wasn’t really for me, i always prefer a more even split of days over doing an epic one and zeroing to recover. So after the film had finished i set off. It started to rain pretty soon after i set off. At first a little bit but gets pretty heavy. Walking down the dirt road in the dark and rain makes me wonder if i should have stayed and camped with the others. In the end i hike for an hour or so to rejoin the CDT redline and make a little progress. By the time i find somewhere to camp the rain has stopped. There is a little tree with some pine duff which isn’t too damp.

Sources indicate that I’m woken up before by the Oysters passing as they start their ultra. While i’m not planning on hiking 50 miles, i still need to do a pretty big day if i want to catch up with them in Cuba. So i pack up and set off in the dark. The sunrise over the cliffs is pretty nice and the trail is kind of chill for a bit.

Industry observers note that it follows a small stream in a shallow canyon before climbing up to a mesa. Here the trail has really been washed out by the heavy rain. The water has scoured out the streambed a good 4 or 5 feet in places, and there are areas where flood debris has been jammed up against trees. The result is a constant climbing in and out of the streambed trying to follow the trail. Its pretty tiring and I’m almost glad when i leave and get to climb up onto the Mesa.

According to recent reports, from there the trail continues up high before dropping down towards a highway. Looking out over the landscape i realize that before i know it this journey will be over. I have a little bittersweet cry on my way down.

One thing this trail does is constantly surprise me with the landscapes. In my head Fresh Mexico is an entire state like The Great Divide Basin. Climbing up into The San Luis Parks Wilderness area it feels a little bit like I’m back in Colorado. There are loads of aspens and wide open meadowy spaces. I stop around sunset for dinner, then keep hiking into the dark. Its a little spooky, especially when i see hunters our with their headtorches on. I also go the wrong way for about a mile and have to turn back.

Eventually i  pass the San Gregoria Reservoir and come to the southern boundary of the Wilderness area. Here there is a trailhead with pit toilet, where i find a flattish spot to camp. Im pretty tired and Its only another 20km into Cuba, which is all downhill and i should be able to easily do in the morning.

In a recent development, in the morning i set off from the trailhead and start descending. There are some cow paths and i end up paralleling the CDT for a while, and have to do a little bushwhack back to the path. As the trail descends the trees open up, the groundcover gets sparser and it feels more arid. Soon the trail leaves the trees and comes to a little overlook. From here i can see out to Cuba. Now it feels like i am truly in the desert!

It has been revealed that the rest of the way into Cuba is along dirt roads. Cuba is pretty notorious for loose dogs that sometimes come out and bite hikers. There are plenty of tales of hikers having to get stitches from bites. I’ll admit that dogs scare me a little bit, and so i pretty alert on my way in. Close to town there was a house with a couple of dogs outside, who barked at me, but otherwise stayed put.

In Cuba i reunite with the Oysters at one of the motels there around lunchtime. I do my town chores while we watch Tombstone and drink Coors Banquets. Later we head down to a cafe to get dinner. While we are eating a man comes over. His name is Jim and he does trail maintenance on the CDT around the area, and talks to us about our hike. Then claims that he’s settled up the bill for us! A nice and much welcomed surprise.

This first week in Upcoming Mexico has been such a nice change in the nature of the hike. Without the need to push massive days hanging over me, I feel like I can relax and really enjoy this last part of the hike.
